input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='README.md'
s=open(p).read()
a='''What a run prints, and what to conclude from it, is
[docs/report-guide.md](docs/report-guide.md).

## Testing
'''
assert s.count(a)==1
s=s.replace(a,'''What a run prints, and what to conclude from it, is
[docs/report-guide.md](docs/report-guide.md).

### Comparing

One invocation's `LSC trimmed` says what that invocation could
resolve, not whether the claim holds across invocations, and a
comparison is a question about two sets of invocations. So record
the runs, repeat them, and let `analyze` read them back:

```
# the benches to compare, in one invocation, repeated five times into one file
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-v2-2t zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst \\
    --record-file runs/control.jsonl
done

# each bench's invocations against themselves: spread, claim, calibration
iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl

# the ladder: each bench against the first, and against the one before
iiac-perf analyze runs/control.jsonl \\
  --compare bench=zcr-mpsc-v2-2t,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop,zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst
```

`--compare KEY=A,B` takes any tag as `KEY`, or `bench`, `host`, or
`file`:

| to compare | run | then |
|---|---|---|
| two benches, or versions of one | them in one invocation, repeated | `--compare bench=A,B` |
| two conditions | each tagged, `--tag cond=A` and `--tag cond=B`, alternating | `--compare cond=A,B` |
| two sessions | each into its own file | `analyze a.jsonl b.jsonl --compare file=a.jsonl,b.jsonl` |

Each row says `detected`, or `not seen, below N%`, what it could
have seen. Benches in one invocation pair by it, and sides that
alternate in time pair as neighbours, so a drift between
invocations cancels. One invocation a side pairs as `one each`,
the weakest claim, so repeat. The notes name any run parameter the
two sides ran differently, and warn when they ran hours apart.

Two builds of the same code can read several percent apart, since
where the code lands in memory moves a bench's level: adding one
function moved `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` by 3.7% on the 3900X. So a variant
of a bench is compared against a `-nop` twin, the same change
doing nothing, and not only against the original. `analyze` is in
[docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md), and the statistics in
[docs/statistics.md](docs/statistics.md).

## Testing
''')
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
vc-x1 validate --fast > tmp/validate.log 2>&1; rc=$?; tail -1 tmp/validate.log; echo rc=$rc

content.text:
Agreed. Naming the sides should be optional when you want all of them. I'll make three forms:

- `--compare` alone compares every bench in the records.
- `--compare KEY` compares every value of that key, `--compare cond` for instance.
- `--compare KEY=A,B` stays as it is, for choosing the sides and their order.

When the values aren't named, they're taken in the order they first ran, so a ladder recorded as `iiac-perf a b c` compares a, then b, then c. For your file, a bare `--compare` gives exactly the line you typed.

Title: `feat: analyze compares two sides`

```
A difference between two versions, two conditions, or two sessions is
the question an experiment asks, and only scripts answered it, each
pairing the sides its own way and none saying when a comparison could
not have seen what it looked for.

* The sides of a comparison have no name.
  - `--compare KEY=A,B` names them by a key, any tag or `bench`,
    `host`, or `file`, so two sessions, two conditions, and two
    benches are one flag. Three or more values are a ladder, each
    against the first and against the one before.
  - `--compare KEY` takes every value the records hold, in the order
    each first ran, and a bare `--compare` every bench.
  - `--compare` repeats, each adding its pairs, so A against B and A
    against C print without B against C.
  - A path given where the sides belong gets the line to run.
* A drift between invocations hides inside an unpaired difference.
  - Invocations sharing a series pair by it, sides alternating in
    time pair as neighbours, and otherwise the groups compare whole,
    or one invocation a side by the claim the two make together.
  - Each row says detected, or not seen and below what percent it
    could have been.
* A difference can come from how the sides ran rather than what they
  ran.
  - Notes name the run parameters the sides ran differently, and warn
    when they ran an hour or more apart, since sessions hours apart
    differ by 0.1 to 0.9% whatever each claims.
  - A comparison with a side too short to trim is counted as left out
    rather than vanishing.
* Whether a comparison finds a known difference was untested.
  - `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-nop` and `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t-store-seqcst`, a new
    bench module beside the untouched base, add a call doing nothing
    and a SeqCst store to each round trip.
  - Five invocations of the three show the base against `-nop`
    3.7% apart, the code's layout alone, and the store 0.45% from
    `-nop`, both detected, so a variant is compared against its
    `-nop` twin.
* A port is only as good as its check.
  - The comparison matches cmp.py on all 28 benches of the two smooth
    sessions, and finds no difference from the sleep in
    clock-shift.jsonl, as clock-shift.py did.
* The group report spaced every row when each bench had one.
  - A blank line parts benches only where a bench has several rows.
```

The README's Comparing section is in the diff too. The body doesn't list docs, following the no-file-list rule.

The pairing holds in every record I checked: `clock_t_ns` has one entry per block, 10 and 10 or 100 and 100, so each block mean gets a time. With that, some thoughts, including the mistakes you expected:

- **The rung's scope changes.** The rung as written ports `make.py`'s seven SVG figures from `docs/statistics.md`, so `make.py` can go at the closing, which the acceptance check needs. Your figure is a different, new one. I'd start with it, as the subcommand's first figure, then port `make.py`'s seven into the same subcommand. It's simpler to begin with, and it builds the SVG plumbing they'll all share.
- **The x axis:**
  - `clock_t_ns` works as the time of each block's seam. It's in ns from the warm's start, so the gaps between points include the block sleeps, 100 to 200 ms under `iiac-perf.toml`. That's right for "does it drift in wall time".
  - To compare the shape of runs, block number is cleaner, since every run lines up block for block. I'd offer both as `--x time|block`, defaulting to `time` as you asked.
  - Two cases need a fallback to block number: `clock_t_ns` is empty when the host exposes no clock, and past 1000 blocks the record merges adjacent blocks (`block_agg`), so the two arrays stop matching.
- **Flag names.** `--benches` and `--runs` already mean something else on a run line: which benches to run, and how many runs. Reusing them for selecting what to plot will confuse, even with per-command help. I'd use:
  - `figures FILE... --bench X,Y`, or the positional pattern `analyze` uses
  - `--show all|trim|extremes|3,1,7` for the runs
- **The run choices:**
  - `all`: every run.
  - `trim`: the kept runs coloured and the dropped ones in faint grey, rather than hiding them. What the trim threw away is half the picture.
  - `max-min`, which I'd call `extremes`: the fastest and slowest runs by mean.
  - A list, `3,1,7`: those runs, coloured in the order given.
- **Several invocations in one file.** Run numbers repeat per invocation, so "run 3" is ambiguous in a five-invocation file, and 50 runs is too many colours. I'd draw one panel per invocation: colours are runs within the invocation, and panels are invocations. `--series ID` picks one.
- **Several benches:** one panel each, never one shared axis. `zcr-mpsc-v2-2t` at 72 ns and `ice-rr-2t` at 1270 ns on one y axis would flatten both.
- **Colours:** about ten that stay distinguishable in light and dark. A ten-run invocation fits, and past ten the colours repeat with a line style.
- **Output:** SVG, written by hand with no new dependency, as `make.py` writes it now. `figures RECORDS OUT_DIR`, as the rung planned, writes one file per figure, and `-o FILE` names the output for a single one.
- **Worth drawing too, cheaply:** each run's trimmed band, and the invocation's trimmed mean as a dashed horizontal line. Then the picture shows the number the report prints.

The plain version: one panel per bench and per invocation, each run a coloured line of block means over time, dropped runs greyed out, as SVG with no new dependencies. Use new flag names so they don't clash with the run flags, and treat this as the first figure of the rung, with `make.py`'s seven to follow.

content.text:
Yes. I can read PNG directly, which is how I checked the figure. SVG I can only read by converting it first. My recommendation:

- **Keep drawing SVG, and rasterize it with the `resvg` crate** when `--out` ends in `.png`. That's a pure-Rust SVG renderer with no system libraries, so the drawing code stays one and PNG is the last step. The format follows the extension, and the default becomes `block-means.png`.
- **Fonts are the one catch.** `resvg` draws text with fonts it finds on the host. A host without fonts, which some headless boxes are, would give a PNG with no labels. Two ways around it:
  1. Load the system fonts, and warn when none are found. Nothing added to the binary.
  2. Embed one font, DejaVu Sans (freely licensed, about 700 KB in the binary), so every host draws the same labels.

  I'd take 2: the same picture on every host is the point of a figure you compare.
- **Cost:** `resvg` brings `usvg`, `tiny-skia`, `fontdb`, and a text shaper, so the build grows by a handful of crates and some compile time. The runtime cost is nothing unless you ask for PNG.
- **The alternative** is shelling out to `rsvg-convert`, which is what I did to look at it. It adds no crate, but depends on a tool the host may not have, so I'd avoid it.

The plain version: yes. The tool keeps drawing SVG and converts it to PNG itself when you name a `.png` file, using a Rust library plus one embedded font, so the labels look the same on every machine.

Figures now render to PNG natively. The full validation passes: 272 tests, and `iiac-perf-dev` is installed at `0.28.18-4`.

- **The format follows `--out`'s extension:** `.png` or `.svg`, anything else refused, with `block-means.png` the default.

  - It adds about 400 KB to the binary, which is now 14.1 MB.
  - The panel titles lost their bold, since only the regular face is embedded.
- **Docs:** `docs/usage.md`, the README example (now `--out control.png`), `--help`, and the rung's record.

iiac-perf-dev figures tmp/control2 --show trim --out tmp/fig.png
